proposals.relationship: Credits reading Marx with opening his path to history through material conditions, class struggle and dialectical thinking.
proposals.evidence_note: His own answer on connection to Marx recounts reading Capital and other named works, crediting his sister Makani Themba and study groups as well as individual reading. He distinguishes a flexible historical method from a fixed set of laws. This self-described formation coexists with his later, Robinson-mediated criticism; no exclusive origin or independent verification of every retrospective date.
primary_locators: Question beginning So we regard you; answer Thanks to my sister; continuation And this is the transition

proposals.relationship: Names Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa as a model that drew him toward historical and revolutionary study.
proposals.evidence_note: In his own named-resources answer, Kelley describes Rodney’s book as opening dependency/underdevelopment literature, then places it with Du Bois and James among three formative historical texts. Samir Amin and Andre Gunder Frank retain credit in that pathway. Original Rodney book remains unread for this dossier; retrospective self-report is not an exclusive genealogy.
primary_locators: Named-resources answer: As I think back; And there were others

proposals.relationship: Credits Black Reconstruction as one of the formative historical models that drew him into the discipline.
proposals.evidence_note: Kelley explicitly names Du Bois’s book alongside James’s Black Jacobins and Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa. The three are co-credited; this is stronger than a shared Black-history topic or bibliographic mention. The original Du Bois book remains unread here.
primary_locators: Named-resources answer: And there were others, notably historians

proposals.relationship: Credits James’s historical and dialectical writings as formative resources for his own historical thinking.
proposals.evidence_note: Kelley names The Black Jacobins among his formative historical models and separately identifies Notes on Dialectics, Spheres of Existence and Facing Reality. He expressly preserves Grace Lee Boggs and Cornelius Castoriadis’s coauthorship of Facing Reality. Specific historical and methodological uses are consolidated; original James books remain unread.
primary_locators: Named-resources answer: I can, however, point; And there were others

proposals.relationship: Names Selections from the Prison Notebooks among the Marxist works that shaped his historical thinking.
proposals.evidence_note: His own answer singles out Gramsci and that work among chief authors/texts, while crediting Luxemburg, James, the Boggses and many others. It establishes an explicit resource without assigning every use of organic intellectuals exclusively to Gramsci: Kelley separately credits Lipsitz’s concrete framework. Original Prison Notebooks remains unread.
primary_locators: Named-resources answer: I can, however, point to the chief Marxist authors

proposals.relationship: Includes Fanon in the political reading through which he developed his approach to Black self-determination and Marxist history.
proposals.evidence_note: Kelley’s answers describe reading Fanon in an All-African People’s Revolutionary Party study group, alongside Nkrumah, Ture, Cabral and Marx. The named-resources answer situates these readings in his effort to connect self-determination, political economy and more than material conditions. No particular Fanon title, formal teacher or exclusive influence is invented; original works unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Scott’s hidden-transcript approach to frame Black working-class politics beyond publicly declared protest.
proposals.evidence_note: The chapter4 opening explicitly quotes Scott’s Domination and the Arts of Resistance and immediately discusses the civil-rights movement as a possible public declaration of hidden transcripts. Kelley qualifies this by stressing earlier organized movements and increasing open conflicts. This selected opening supports conceptual use, not a simple evolution from silence to revolt. Full chapter/book and original Scott text remain unread.
primary_locators: Race Rebels chapter4 opening, Scott epigraph and first complete paragraph

proposals.relationship: Through Robinson’s criticism, questions Marx’s placement of unfree labor and anticolonial revolt at the margins of modern capitalism.
proposals.evidence_note: In his own racial-capitalism answer, Kelley quotes and develops Cedric Robinson’s criticism of primitive accumulation and universal proletarian models, then expressly identifies lapses in Marx’s account of colonial capitalism. He also insists Marx opposed slavery/colonialism and wrote within a stated scope. This qualified, Robinson-mediated criticism coexists with formative use; it is not a rejection of all Marx or an independent new reading of the originals.
primary_locators: Racial-capitalism answer: Robinson takes Marx and Engels to task; final And Marx’s argument

proposals.relationship: Brundage compares Race Rebels with Beyond a Boundary for their accounts of marginalized people’s cultural creativity and agency.
proposals.evidence_note: The signed review opening explicitly compares the two books’ bold yet nuanced methods and attention to rebellious inventiveness. This is Brundage’s bounded comparison, not his proof that Beyond a Boundary caused Race Rebels or that every argument is identical. Kelley’s own stated use of other James works is separately sourced. Original books remain unread.
